extracted.intended_audience: general public; Texas residents; legal observers; anime/manga and creative communities
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and explain Texas Senate Bill 20 (2025), a state law creating criminal offenses related to 'obscene visual material' that appears to depict a child, including AI-generated, animated, and cartoon images, and describe reactions, penalties, and potential impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of new criminal offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Creates new criminal offenses for 'obscene visual material' and possession or promotion of 'obscene visual material' that appears to depict a child under age 18.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article summary and long title state the law 'Relating to the creation of the criminal offense of possession, promotion, or production of certain obscene visual material appearing to depict a child.' The law is described as applying whether the image is of an actual person, animated/cartoon, or AI-generated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered acts: possession, promotion, production, viewing
rubrics_metrics.description: The law targets those who possess, promote, produce, or view visual material deemed obscene which is said to depict a child.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long title and summary list 'possession, promotion, or production' and the summary also mentions 'possess, promote, or view' — indicating multiple forms of handling such material are criminalized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age threshold for depicted person
rubrics_metrics.description: Applies to material that 'appears to depict a child under age 18.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute uses 'appears to depict' and sets the age boundary at under 18, making the presence/appearance of youth the relevant element rather than an actual minor necessarily being involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of media covered (actual, animated, AI-generated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Includes images of actual persons, animated or cartoon depictions, and images created through computer software or artificial intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law explicitly covers AI-created images and deepfakes; supporters tout it as addressing AI-generated child pornography while critics worry about non-photographic media (anime, manga, graphic novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity / 'appears to depict' subjective standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses the terms 'obscene visual material' and material that 'appears to depict' a child — language described as broad and subjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argue the wording is 'vague and open to interpretation' as to what is considered obscene or 'appears' to be child-like, raising concerns about inconsistent enforcement and overbreadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties and sentencing
rubrics_metrics.description: Those charged with the felony offense could face state jail, potentially elevated with prior conviction, a $10,000 fine and two years in prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions state possible state jail time; the page notes elevation if the person has a prior conviction and lists a $10,000 fine and two years in prison as potential consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased enforcement powers for police
rubrics_metrics.description: S.B. 20 'gives Texas police more provisions to restrict artificial intelligence-created child pornography.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill is described as creating new criminal charges and expanding tools available to law enforcement to address AI-created images and deepfakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional / First Amendment concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics describe the law as unconstitutional, arguing it violates the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment and conflicts with Ashcroft v. Free Speech Coalition precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal organizations (e.g., Comic Book Legal Defense Fund) warned about unconstitutional prosecutions for possessing certain cartoons or animation; commentators cite established case law limiting restrictions on non-obscene virtual depictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of chilling effect on creative media
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad language could have a chilling effect on anime, manga, graphic novels, and other media produced, distributed, or created within Texas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple commentators, retailers, and convention organizers expressed concern that artists and fans might self-censor or that works could be pulled from stores or events (examples: bans at conventions; Dragon Ball issues pulled from shelves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity leading to potential overcriminalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns that vague wording could 'criminalize certain forms' of anime, manga, video games, and artistic expression and be used beyond intended targets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and warnings from scholars, activists, and industry figures predict prosecutions or removals of mainstream titles where youthfulness or non-sexual contexts could be misread as 'obscene' or child-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic value as a possible determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion includes suggestion that state officials might deem works exempt or not depending on whether they have 'artistic value.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commentary (e.g., Screen Rant analysis) hypothesizes that enforcement discretion could turn on 'artistic value,' though the statute's text and standards for such determinations are criticized as unclear.
